title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 4
paragraphs: Bald Hills, Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky's estate, lay forty miles east of Smolensk and two miles from the main road to Moscow.

That same evening the prince gave his instructions to Alpatych, Dessalles asked to see Princess Mary and told her that, since the prince was not well and was taking no steps to ensure his safety, and since Prince Andrew's letter made it clear that staying at Bald Hills might be dangerous, he respectfully advised her to send a letter with Alpatych to the Provincial Governor at Smolensk, asking about the state of affairs and the extent of the danger to Bald Hills. Dessalles wrote this letter for Princess Mary, she signed it, and it was given to Alpatych with instructions to hand it to the Governor and return as quickly as possible if there was danger.

Having received all his orders, Alpatych put on a white beaver hat—a present from the prince—and carrying a stick as the prince did, went out accompanied by his family. Three well-fed roan horses stood harnessed to a small covered carriage.

The large bell was muffled and the small bells on the harness were stuffed with paper. The prince allowed no one at Bald Hills to drive with ringing bells, but on a long journey Alpatych liked to have them. His entourage—the senior clerk, a counting-house clerk, a scullery maid, a cook, two old women, a little page boy, the coachman, and various household servants—were seeing him off.

His daughter arranged chintz-covered down cushions for him to sit on and placed one behind his back. His old sister-in-law slipped in a small bundle, and one of the coachmen helped him into the carriage.
"There! There! Women's fussing! Women, women!" said Alpatych, puffing and speaking rapidly just as the prince did, and he climbed into the carriage.
After giving the clerk orders about the work to be done, Alpatych—no longer imitating the prince—lifted the hat from his bald head and crossed himself three times.
"If there's anything... come back, Yakov Alpatych! For Christ's sake, think of us!" cried his wife, referring to the rumors of war and the enemy.

"Women, women! Women's fussing!" muttered Alpatych to himself and set off on his journey, gazing at the fields of yellow rye and the still-green, thickly growing oats, and at other quite black fields just being plowed for the second time.

As he rode along, he looked with pleasure at the year's splendid crop of grain, studied the strips of rye already being harvested here and there, made his mental calculations about the sowing and the harvest, and checked whether he had forgotten any of the prince's orders.
Having fed the horses twice along the way, he arrived at the town toward evening on the fourth of August.

Alpatych kept meeting and passing baggage trains and troops on the road. As he approached Smolensk, he heard the sounds of distant gunfire, but these didn't impress him. What struck him most was the sight of a splendid field of oats in which a military camp had been pitched and which was being mowed down by the soldiers, obviously for fodder. This fact impressed Alpatych, but thinking about his own business he soon forgot it.

All the concerns of his life for more than thirty years had been bounded by the prince's will, and he never stepped beyond those limits. Anything not connected with carrying out the prince's orders didn't interest him and didn't even exist for Alpatych.

On reaching Smolensk on the evening of the fourth of August, he put up in the Gachina district across the Dnieper, at the inn kept by Ferapontov, where he had stayed for the last thirty years. Some thirty years ago, on Alpatych's advice, Ferapontov had bought a piece of forest from the prince, started trading, and now had a house, an inn, and a grain shop in the province. He was a stout, dark, red-faced peasant in his forties, with thick lips, a broad knob of a nose, similar knobs over his black frowning brows, and a round belly.
Wearing a waistcoat over his cotton shirt, Ferapontov was standing in front of his shop, which faced the street. Seeing Alpatych, he went up to him.
"You're welcome, Yakov Alpatych. Folks are leaving town, and you've come to it," said he.
"Why are they leaving town?" asked Alpatych.
"That's what I say. People are foolish! Always scared of the French."
"Women's fussing, women's fussing!" said Alpatych.
"Just what I think, Yakov Alpatych. What I say is: the orders are not to let them in, so that must be right. And the peasants are charging three rubles for carting—it's not Christian!"
Yakov Alpatych heard without really listening. He ordered a samovar and hay for his horses, and after having his tea, went to bed.

All night long troops were moving past the inn. The next morning Alpatych put on the jacket he wore only in town and went out on business. It was a sunny morning and by eight o'clock it was already hot. "A good day for harvesting," thought Alpatych.

From beyond the town, firing had been heard since early morning. By eight o'clock the boom of cannon was added to the sound of musket fire. Many people were hurrying through the streets and there were soldiers everywhere, but cabs were still driving about, shopkeepers stood at their doors, and church services were being held as usual. Alpatych went to the shops, to government offices, to the post office, and to the Governor's. In the offices and shops and at the post office, everyone was talking about the army and the enemy who was already attacking the town—everyone was asking what should be done, and all were trying to calm one another.

In front of the Governor's house, Alpatych found a large crowd of people, Cossacks, and one of the Governor's traveling carriages. At the entrance he met two local landowners, one of whom he knew. This man, a former captain of police, was saying angrily:

"It's no joke, you know! It's fine if you're single. 'One man ruined is just one man,' as the saying goes, but with thirteen in your family and all your property... They've brought us to utter ruin! What kind of governors are these? They should be hanged—the criminals!"
"Oh come, that's enough!" said the other.
"What do I care? Let him hear! We're not dogs," said the former police captain, and looking around, he noticed Alpatych.
"Oh, Yakov Alpatych! What brings you here?"

"To see the Governor, on his excellency's orders," answered Alpatych, lifting his chin and proudly thrusting his hand into the front of his coat as he always did when mentioning the prince. "He has ordered me to inquire into the state of affairs," he added.

"Yes, go and find out!" shouted the angry gentleman. "They've let things get to the point where there are no carts or anything!... There it is again, do you hear?" he said, pointing in the direction of the gunfire.
"They've brought us all to ruin... the criminals!" he repeated, and went down the steps.

Alpatych shook his head and went upstairs. In the waiting room were shopkeepers, women, and officials, all silently looking at one another. The door of the Governor's office opened and they all rose and pressed forward. An official ran out, said a few words to a merchant, called a stout official wearing a cross on his neck to follow him, and vanished again, clearly trying to avoid the inquiring looks and questions aimed at him. Alpatych stepped forward, and the next time the official emerged, he addressed him with one hand placed inside his buttoned coat, handing over two letters.
"To his Honor Baron Asch, from General-in-Chief Prince Bolkonsky," he announced with such solemnity and importance that the official turned to him and took the letters.
A few minutes later the Governor received Alpatych and hurriedly said:

"Inform the prince and princess that I knew nothing—I was acting on the highest instructions—here..." and he handed Alpatych a document. "Still, as the prince is unwell, my advice is that they should go to Moscow. I'm about to leave myself. Inform them..."
But the Governor didn't finish: a dusty, sweating officer ran into the room and began speaking rapidly in French. The Governor's face expressed terror.
"Go," he said, nodding to Alpatych, and began questioning the officer.

Anxious, frightened, helpless glances were turned on Alpatych when he came out of the Governor's office. Now involuntarily listening to the gunfire, which had drawn nearer and grown louder, Alpatych hurried back to his inn. The paper from the Governor said this:

"I assure you that the town of Smolensk is not in the slightest danger as yet and it is unlikely that it will be threatened. I from one side and Prince Bagration from the other are marching to unite our forces before Smolensk, which junction will be effected on the 22nd instant, and both armies with their united forces will defend our compatriots of the province entrusted to your care till our efforts shall have beaten back the enemies of our Fatherland, or till the last warrior in our valiant ranks has perished. From this you will see that you have every right to reassure the inhabitants of Smolensk, for those defended by two such brave armies may feel assured of victory." (Instructions from Barclay de Tolly to Baron Asch, the civil governor of Smolensk, 1812.)
People were anxiously roaming about the streets.

Carts piled high with household goods—chairs, cupboards—kept emerging from the yards and moving along the streets. Loaded carts stood at the house next to Ferapontov's, and women were wailing and weeping as they said goodbye. A small dog ran barking around in front of the harnessed horses.

Alpatych entered the inn yard at a quicker pace than usual and went straight to the shed where his horses and carriage were. The coachman was asleep. He woke him up, told him to harness the horses, and went into the building. From the innkeeper's room came the sounds of a child crying, the desperate sobs of a woman, and the hoarse, angry shouting of Ferapontov. The cook came running through the passage like a frightened hen, just as Alpatych entered.
"He's beaten her to death. Killed the mistress!... Beat her... dragged her around!"
"What for?" asked Alpatych.

"She kept begging to leave. She's a woman! 'Take me away,' she says, 'don't let me die with my little children! Everyone else has gone,' she says, 'so why don't we go?' And he started beating her and dragging her around!"
At these words Alpatych nodded as if in approval, and not wanting to hear more, went to the door of the room across from the innkeeper's, where he had left his purchases.
"You brute, you murderer!" screamed a thin, pale woman who, with a baby in her arms and her headscarf torn off, burst through the door at that moment and ran down the steps into the yard.
Ferapontov came out after her, but seeing Alpatych, he adjusted his waistcoat, smoothed his hair, yawned, and followed Alpatych into the opposite room.
"Leaving already?" he said.
Alpatych, without answering or looking at his host, sorted his packages and asked how much he owed.
"We'll settle up! Well, did you see the Governor?" asked Ferapontov. "What's been decided?"
Alpatych replied that the Governor hadn't told him anything definite.

"With our kind of business, how can we just leave?" said Ferapontov. "We'd have to pay seven rubles a cartload to Dorogobutz, and I tell them it's not Christian to charge that! Selivanov, now, he made a good deal last Thursday—sold flour to the army at nine rubles a sack. Will you have some tea?" he added.
While the horses were being harnessed, Alpatych and Ferapontov drank tea and talked about the price of grain, the crops, and the good weather for harvesting.

"Well, it seems to be getting quieter," remarked Ferapontov, finishing his third cup of tea and getting up. "Our boys must have gotten the upper hand. They had orders not to let them in. So we've got the strength, it seems... They say the other day Platov drove them into the river Marina and drowned some eighteen thousand in one day."

Alpatych collected his parcels, handed them to the coachman who had come in, and settled up with the innkeeper. The noise of wheels, hooves, and bells was heard from the gateway as his little carriage drove out.

It was by now late in the afternoon. Half the street was in shadow, the other half brightly lit by the sun. Alpatych looked out of the window and went to the door. Suddenly the strange sound of a far-off whistling and thud was heard, followed by a boom of cannon blending into a dull roar that set the windows rattling.

He went out into the street: two men were running past toward the bridge. From different directions came whistling sounds and the thud of cannon balls and bursting shells falling on the town. But these sounds were barely noticed compared to the noise of the firing outside the town and drew little attention from the inhabitants. The town was being bombarded by a hundred and thirty guns that Napoleon had ordered up after four o'clock. The people didn't immediately grasp the meaning of this bombardment.

At first the noise of falling bombs and shells only aroused curiosity. Ferapontov's wife, who until then had not stopped wailing under the shed, became quiet and, with the baby in her arms, went to the gate, listening to the sounds and gazing in silence at the people.

The cook and a shop assistant came to the gate. With lively curiosity everyone tried to catch a glimpse of the projectiles as they flew overhead. Several people came around the corner talking excitedly.
"What power!" remarked one. "Smashed the roof and ceiling to splinters!"
"Plowed up the ground like a pig," said another.
"That's the stuff—gets the blood going!" laughed the first. "Lucky you jumped aside, or it would have flattened you!"

Others joined them and stopped to tell how cannon balls had fallen on a house close by. Meanwhile still more projectiles—now with the swift, sinister whistle of a cannon ball, now with the agreeable intermittent whistle of a shell—flew over people's heads incessantly, but not one fell nearby; they all flew over. Alpatych was getting into his carriage. The innkeeper stood at the gate.
"What are you staring at?" he shouted at the cook, who in her red skirt with sleeves rolled up, bare elbows swinging, had stepped to the corner to listen to what was being said.
"What a sight!" she exclaimed, but hearing her master's voice, she turned back, pulling down her tucked-up skirt.
Once more something whistled, but this time much closer, swooping down like a little bird; a flame flashed in the middle of the street, something exploded, and the street was shrouded in smoke.
"Scoundrel, what are you doing?" shouted the innkeeper, rushing to the cook.

At that moment the pitiful wailing of women was heard from different directions, the frightened baby began to cry, and people crowded silently with pale faces around the cook. The loudest sound in that crowd was her wailing.
"Oh-h-h! Dear souls, dear kind souls! Don't let me die! My good souls!..."

Five minutes later no one remained in the street. The cook, with her thigh broken by a shell fragment, had been carried into the kitchen. Alpatych, his coachman, Ferapontov's wife and children, and the house porter were all sitting in the cellar, listening. The roar of guns, the whistling of projectiles, and the pitiful moaning of the cook—which rose above the other sounds—did not stop for a moment. The mistress rocked and hushed her baby and when anyone came into the cellar asked in a pathetic whisper what had become of her husband, who had stayed in the street. A shopman who entered told her that her husband had gone with others to the cathedral, from where they were fetching the miracle-working icon of Smolensk.

Toward dusk the cannonade began to die down. Alpatych left the cellar and stood in the doorway. The evening sky that had been so clear was clouded with smoke, through which, high up, the crescent of the new moon shone strangely. Now that the terrible din of the guns had ceased, a hush seemed to reign over the town, broken only by the rustle of footsteps, the moaning, the distant cries, and the crackling of fires that seemed to be everywhere. The cook's moans had now subsided. On two sides, black curling clouds of smoke rose and spread from the fires. Through the streets, soldiers in various uniforms walked or ran in all directions like ants from a ruined anthill. Several of them ran into Ferapontov's yard before Alpatych's eyes. Alpatych went out to the gate. A retreating regiment, crowding and hurrying, blocked the street.
Noticing him, an officer said: "The town is being abandoned. Get out, get out!" and then, turning to the soldiers, shouted:
"I'll teach you to run into people's yards!"

Alpatych went back inside, called the coachman, and told him to get moving. Ferapontov's whole household came out too, following Alpatych and the coachman. The women, who had been silent until then, suddenly began to wail as they looked at the fires—the smoke and even the flames of which could be seen in the fading twilight—and as if in answer, the same kind of wailing was heard from other parts of the street. Inside the shed, Alpatych and the coachman arranged the tangled reins and traces of their horses with trembling hands.

As Alpatych was driving out of the gate, he saw about ten soldiers in Ferapontov's open shop, talking loudly and filling their bags and packs with flour and sunflower seeds. Just then Ferapontov returned and entered his shop. Seeing the soldiers, he started to shout at them, but suddenly stopped and, clutching at his hair, burst into sobs and laughter:
"Take it all, boys! Don't let those devils get it!" he cried, grabbing some bags of flour himself and throwing them into the street.
Some of the soldiers were frightened and ran away; others went on filling their bags. Seeing Alpatych, Ferapontov turned to him:
"Russia is done for!" he cried. "Alpatych, I'll set the place on fire myself. We're done for!" and Ferapontov ran into the yard.

Soldiers were passing in a constant stream along the street, completely blocking it, so that Alpatych couldn't get out and had to wait. Ferapontov's wife and children were also sitting in a cart, waiting until they could drive out.

Night had come. There were stars in the sky and the new moon shone out through the smoke that screened it. On the sloping descent to the Dnieper, Alpatych's cart and the innkeeper's wife's cart, slowly moving among the rows of soldiers and other vehicles, had to stop. In a side street near the crossroads where the vehicles had stopped, a house and some shops were on fire. The fire was already burning itself out. The flames would die down and disappear in black smoke, then suddenly flare up again, lighting with strange clarity the faces of the people crowding at the crossroads. Dark figures moved about before the fire, and through the incessant crackling of the flames, talking and shouting could be heard. Seeing that his carriage couldn't move for some time, Alpatych got down and turned into the side street to look at the fire. Soldiers were constantly rushing back and forth, and he saw two of them and a man in a rough coat dragging burning beams into another yard across the street, while others carried bundles of hay.

Alpatych went up to a large crowd standing before a tall barn that was blazing fiercely. The walls were all on fire, the back wall had collapsed, the wooden roof was caving in, and the rafters were ablaze. The crowd was obviously watching for the roof to fall, and Alpatych watched for it too.
"Alpatych!" a familiar voice suddenly called out to the old man.
"Your excellency! Mercy on us!" answered Alpatych, immediately recognizing the voice of his young prince.
Prince Andrew, in his riding cloak and mounted on a black horse, was looking at Alpatych from the back of the crowd.
"Why are you here?" he asked.
"Your... your excellency," stammered Alpatych and broke into sobs. "Are we really lost? Master!..."
"Why are you here?" Prince Andrew repeated.
At that moment the flames flared up and illuminated his young master's pale, worn face. Alpatych told how he had been sent to Smolensk and how difficult it was to get away.
"Are we really completely lost, your excellency?" he asked again.
Prince Andrew, without answering, took out a notebook, raised his knee, and began writing in pencil on a page he tore out. He wrote to his sister:
"Smolensk is being abandoned. Bald Hills will be occupied by the enemy within a week. Leave immediately for Moscow. Let me know at once when you start. Send word by special messenger to Usvyazh."

Having written this and given the paper to Alpatych, he told him how to arrange for the departure of the prince, the princess, his son, and the boy's tutor, and how and where to let him know immediately. Before he had finished giving these instructions, a chief of staff followed by his suite galloped up to him.

"You are a colonel?" shouted the chief of staff in a voice with a German accent, familiar to Prince Andrew. "Houses are being set on fire in your presence and you just stand by! What does this mean? You will answer for it!" shouted Berg, who was now assistant to the chief of staff of the left flank of the first army's infantry—a position which, as Berg put it, was "very pleasant and well in view."
Prince Andrew looked at him and, without replying, went on speaking to Alpatych.
"So tell them that I will wait for a reply until the tenth, and if by the tenth I don't get word that they've all left, I'll have to drop everything and come to Bald Hills myself."
"Prince," said Berg, recognizing Prince Andrew, "I only spoke because I have to follow orders, because I always follow them exactly... You must please excuse me," he went on apologetically.
Something cracked in the flames. The fire died down for a moment and wreaths of black smoke rolled from under the roof. There was another terrible crash and something huge collapsed.

"Ou-rou-rou!" yelled the crowd, echoing the crash of the collapsing barn roof, from which the burning grain gave off a cake-like aroma all around. The flames flared up again, lighting the animated, delighted, exhausted faces of the spectators.
The man in the rough coat raised his arms and shouted:
"It's going great, boys! Now it's really blazing... Beautiful!"
"That's the owner himself," cried several voices.
"Well then," continued Prince Andrew to Alpatych, "tell them everything I've said"; and without a word to Berg, who stood mute beside him, he touched his horse and rode down the side street.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 14
paragraphs: "So, is she pretty? Oh, friend—my pink one is delicious; her name's Dunyasha..."
But glancing at Rostov's face, Ilyin stopped short. He could see that his hero and commander was following an entirely different train of thought.
Rostov glanced angrily at Ilyin and without replying strode rapidly toward the village.
"I'll show them; I'll give it to them, the scoundrels!" he said to himself.
Alpatych, at a gliding trot, just barely managing not to run, kept up with him with difficulty.
"What decision have you been pleased to reach?" he said.
Rostov stopped and, clenching his fists, suddenly turned on Alpatych with fierce intensity.

"Decision? What decision? Old fool!" he cried. "What have you been doing? The peasants are rioting and you can't control them? You're a traitor yourself! I know you. I'll skin you all alive!" And as if afraid of wasting his store of anger, he left Alpatych and strode rapidly forward. Alpatych, mastering his offended feelings, kept pace with Rostov at a gliding gait and continued to share his views. He said the peasants were obstinate and that at this moment it would be unwise to confront them without armed force—wouldn't it be better to send for the military first?
"I'll give them armed force... I'll confront them!" Rostov uttered meaninglessly, breathless with irrational animal fury and the need to vent it.

Without thinking about what he would do, he moved unconsciously with quick, resolute steps toward the crowd. And the closer he got, the more Alpatych felt that this reckless action might actually produce good results. The peasants in the crowd were similarly affected when they saw Rostov's rapid, firm steps and resolute, frowning face.

After the hussars had come to the village and Rostov had gone to see the princess, a certain confusion and division had arisen among the crowd. Some peasants said these newcomers were Russians and might take offense that the mistress was being detained. Dron shared this opinion, but as soon as he expressed it, Karp and others attacked their former Elder.

"How many years have you been fattening off the commune?" Karp shouted at him. "It's all the same to you! You'll dig up your buried pot of money and take it with you... What do you care whether our homes are destroyed or not?"
"We were told to keep order, that nobody's to leave their homes or take a single grain—and that's that!" cried another.

"It was your son's turn to be drafted, but oh no! You were too stingy to part with your big lump of a boy," a little old man suddenly began attacking Dron—"so they took my Vanka and shaved him for a soldier! But we all have to die."
"Sure, we all have to die. I'm not against the commune," said Dron.
"That's right—not against it! You've stuffed your belly..."

The two tall peasants had their say. As soon as Rostov, followed by Ilyin, Lavrushka, and Alpatych, came up to the crowd, Karp, thrusting his fingers into his belt and smiling slightly, moved to the front. Dron, on the contrary, slipped to the rear, and the crowd drew closer together.
"Who's your Elder here? Hey!" shouted Rostov, coming up to the crowd with quick steps.
"The Elder? What do you want with him?" asked Karp.
But before the words were fully out of his mouth, his cap flew off and a fierce blow jerked his head to one side.
"Caps off, traitors!" shouted Rostov furiously. "Where's the Elder?" he demanded.
"The Elder... He wants the Elder!... Dron Zakharych, you!" meek and flustered voices were heard here and there, and caps began to come off.
"We're not rioting, we're following orders," declared Karp, and at that moment several voices began speaking at once.
"It's as the old men decided—there's too many of you giving orders."

"Arguing? Mutiny!... Traitors!" cried Rostov meaninglessly in a voice not his own, gripping Karp by the collar. "Tie him up! Tie him up!" he shouted, though there was no one to do it except Lavrushka and Alpatych.
Lavrushka, however, ran up to Karp and seized his arms from behind.
"Shall I call our men from beyond the hill?" he called out.
Alpatych turned to the peasants and ordered two of them by name to come and bind Karp. The men obediently stepped out of the crowd and began taking off their belts.
"Where's the Elder?" demanded Rostov in a loud voice.
With a pale and frowning face, Dron stepped out of the crowd.
"Are you the Elder? Bind him, Lavrushka!" shouted Rostov, as if that command too could not possibly meet with any resistance.
And in fact two more peasants began tying Dron, who took off his own belt and handed it to them, as if to help.
"And all of you—listen to me!" said Rostov to the peasants. "Get back to your homes at once, and don't let me hear another word out of you!"
"Why, we haven't done anything wrong! We were just being foolish. It's all nonsense... I said at the time it wasn't proper," voices were heard grumbling.
"There! What did I tell you?" said Alpatych, coming into his own again. "It's wrong, boys!"
"All our foolishness, Yakov Alpatych," came the answers, and the crowd immediately began to disperse through the village.
The two bound men were led off to the manor house. The two drunken peasants followed them.
"Aye, look at you!" said one of them to Karp.
"How can you talk to the masters like that? What were you thinking, you fool?" added the other. "A real fool!"

Two hours later the carts stood in the courtyard of the Bogucharovo house. The peasants were briskly carrying out the proprietor's belongings and loading them onto the carts, and Dron, freed at Princess Mary's request from the room where he had been locked up, stood in the yard directing the men.

"Don't just throw it in like that," said one peasant, a man with a round, smiling face, taking a casket from a housemaid. "That cost good money! You can't just chuck it in or shove it under the rope where it'll get scratched. I don't like sloppy work. Let it all be done properly, by the book. Look—put it under the bast matting and cover it with hay—that's the way!"
"Books, books!" said another peasant, carrying out Prince Andrew's bookcases. "Careful—don't bump it! Heavy stuff, boys—solid books."
"Yes, they worked all day and never played!" remarked the tall, round-faced peasant gravely, pointing with a knowing wink at the dictionaries stacked on top.

Not wanting to impose himself on the princess, Rostov didn't return to the house but stayed in the village to wait for her departure. When her carriage drove out, he mounted up and accompanied her eight miles from Bogucharovo to where the road was held by their own troops. At the inn at Yankovo he respectfully took his leave, for the first time allowing himself to kiss her hand.

"How can you say such things!" he said, blushing, in reply to Princess Mary's expressions of gratitude for her rescue, as she called what had happened. "Any policeman would have done the same! If we only had peasants to fight, we wouldn't have let the enemy get this far," he said with a sense of embarrassment and a desire to change the subject. "I'm only glad to have had the chance to meet you. Goodbye, Princess. I wish you happiness and consolation, and hope to see you again in happier circumstances. If you don't want to make me blush, please don't thank me!"

But the princess, even if she didn't thank him again in words, thanked him with her whole expression—her face radiant with gratitude and tenderness. She couldn't believe there was nothing to thank him for. On the contrary, she felt certain that if he hadn't been there, she would have been lost to the mutineers and the French, and that he had exposed himself to terrible and obvious danger to save her. Even more certain was she that he was a man of noble and lofty soul, able to understand her situation and her grief. His kind, honest eyes, with tears rising in them when she herself began to cry as she spoke of her loss, never left her memory.
When she had said goodbye and was alone, she suddenly felt her eyes filling with tears, and then, for the first time, a strange question presented itself: did she love him?

On the rest of the journey to Moscow, though her situation was not a cheerful one, Dunyasha, who rode with her in the carriage, more than once noticed that her mistress leaned out the window and smiled with an expression of mingled joy and sorrow.
"Well, suppose I do love him?" thought Princess Mary.

Ashamed as she was of admitting to herself that she had fallen in love with a man who might never love her back, she comforted herself with the thought that no one would ever know, and that she would not be to blame if, without ever speaking of it to anyone, she continued to the end of her life to love the man with whom she had fallen in love for the first and last time.

Sometimes when she recalled his looks, his sympathy, and his words, happiness did not seem impossible. It was at those moments that Dunyasha noticed her mistress smiling as she looked out the carriage window.
"Was it not fate that brought him to Bogucharovo, at that very moment?" thought Princess Mary. "And that made his sister refuse my brother?" In all this Princess Mary saw the hand of Providence.

The impression the princess made on Rostov was a very pleasant one. To remember her gave him pleasure, and when his comrades, hearing of his adventure at Bogucharovo, teased him about going to look for hay and instead picking up one of the wealthiest heiresses in Russia, he grew angry. He was angry precisely because the idea of marrying the gentle Princess Mary—who attracted him and had an enormous fortune—had more than once entered his mind against his will. For himself personally, Nicholas could not have wished for a better wife: marrying her would make his mother happy, would set his father's affairs in order, and would even—he felt it—ensure Princess Mary's happiness.
But Sonya? And his promise? That was why Rostov got angry when they teased him about Princess Bolkonskaya.

title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 25
paragraphs: The officers were about to leave, but Prince Andrew, apparently reluctant to be left alone with his friend, asked them to stay and have tea. Seats were brought and tea was served. The officers gazed with surprise at Pierre's huge, stout figure and listened to his talk about Moscow and the position of their army, around which he had ridden. Prince Andrew remained silent, and his expression was so forbidding that Pierre directed his remarks mainly to the good-natured battalion commander.
"So you understand the whole layout of our troops?" Prince Andrew interrupted him.
"Yes—that is, how do you mean?" said Pierre. "Not being a military man, I can't say I've fully understood it, but I get the general picture."
"Well then, you know more than anyone else, whoever that may be," said Prince Andrew.
"Oh!" said Pierre, looking over his spectacles in perplexity at Prince Andrew. "Well, and what do you think about Kutuzov's appointment?" he asked.
"I was very glad of his appointment, that's all I know," replied Prince Andrew.
"And tell me your opinion of Barclay de Tolly. In Moscow they're saying all sorts of things about him... What do you think of him?"
"Ask them," replied Prince Andrew, indicating the officers.
Pierre looked at Timokhin with the condescendingly inquiring smile that everyone involuntarily used when addressing that officer.
"We can see the light again since his Serenity's been appointed, your excellency," said Timokhin timidly, continually glancing at his colonel.
"Why so?" asked Pierre.

"Well, take just firewood and fodder, for example. Why, when we were retreating from Sventsyani, we didn't dare touch a stick or a wisp of hay or anything. You see, we were leaving, so he'd get it all; isn't that right, your excellency?" and Timokhin again looked at the prince. "But we didn't dare. In our regiment two officers were court-martialed for that kind of thing. But once his Serenity took command, everything became straightforward. Now we can see the light..."
"Then why was it forbidden?"
Timokhin looked about in confusion, not knowing how to answer. Pierre put the same question to Prince Andrew.

"So as not to lay waste the country we were leaving to the enemy," said Prince Andrew with bitter irony. "It's very sound: you can't allow the land to be pillaged or accustom the troops to looting. At Smolensk too he calculated correctly that the French might outflank us since they had larger forces. But he couldn't understand this," cried Prince Andrew in a shrill voice that seemed to escape him involuntarily: "he couldn't understand that there, for the first time, we were fighting for Russian soil, and that there was a spirit in the men such as I had never seen before, and that we had held the French for two days, and that that success had increased our strength tenfold. He ordered us to retreat, and all our efforts and losses went for nothing. He didn't intend to betray us; he tried to do his best; he thought out everything carefully—and that is exactly why he's unfit. He's unfit now precisely because he plans everything very thoroughly and precisely, as every German must. How can I explain it?... Well, say your father has a German valet, and the valet is excellent and satisfies your father's needs better than you could—then it's fine to let him serve. But if your father is mortally ill, you'll send the valet away and attend to your father with your own clumsy, unpracticed hands, and will comfort him better than a skilled stranger could. That's how it's been with Barclay. While Russia was healthy, a foreigner could serve her and be a splendid minister; but the moment she's in danger, she needs one of her own. But in your Club they've been calling him a traitor! They've slandered him as a traitor, and the only result will be that later, ashamed of their false accusations, they'll suddenly make him out to be a hero or genius instead—and that will be even more unjust. He is an honest and very meticulous German."
"And they say he's a skillful commander," Pierre remarked.
"I don't understand what 'a skillful commander' means," replied Prince Andrew ironically.
"A skillful commander?" said Pierre. "Well, one who foresees all possibilities... and anticipates the enemy's intentions."
"But that's impossible," said Prince Andrew, as if it were a long-settled matter.
Pierre looked at him in surprise.
"And yet they say war is like a game of chess?" he remarked.

"Yes," replied Prince Andrew, "but with this little difference: in chess you can think over each move as long as you like and aren't limited by time, and with this further difference, that a knight is always stronger than a pawn and two pawns are always stronger than one—while in war a battalion is sometimes stronger than a division and sometimes weaker than a company. The relative strength of bodies of troops can never be known to anyone. Believe me," he continued, "if things depended on plans made by the staff, I would be there making plans. But instead I have the honor of serving here in the regiment with these gentlemen, and I believe that on us—not on those others—tomorrow's battle will depend... Success never has depended, and never will depend, on position, equipment, or even numbers—and least of all on position."
"But on what then?"
"On the feeling that is in me and in him," he pointed to Timokhin, "and in every soldier."

Prince Andrew glanced at Timokhin, who looked at his commander in alarm and confusion. In contrast to his former reserved taciturnity, Prince Andrew now seemed stirred up. He apparently couldn't stop himself from expressing the thoughts that had suddenly taken hold of him.

"A battle is won by those who firmly resolve to win it! Why did we lose the battle of Austerlitz? Our losses were nearly equal to the French, but very early we told ourselves we were losing the battle—and we lost it. And we said so because we had nothing to fight for there, we wanted to get away from the battlefield as fast as possible. 'We've lost, so let's run,' and we ran. If we hadn't said that till evening, God knows what might have happened. But tomorrow we won't say it! You talk about our position—the left flank weak, the right flank overextended," he went on. "That's all nonsense, none of it matters. But what awaits us tomorrow? A hundred million totally unpredictable circumstances that will be decided in an instant by whether our men or theirs run or don't run, and whether this man or that man is killed. Everything being done now is just play. The fact is that those men you've been riding around with don't just fail to help—they actually hinder. They're only concerned with their own petty interests."
"At such a moment?" said Pierre reproachfully.

"At such a moment!" Prince Andrew repeated. "To them it's only an opportunity to undermine a rival and earn an extra medal or ribbon. For me, tomorrow means this: a Russian army of a hundred thousand and a French army of a hundred thousand have met to fight, and the point is that these two hundred thousand men will fight, and whichever side fights more fiercely and spares itself less will win. And if you want to know: whatever happens, whatever blunders those at the top may make, we will win tomorrow's battle. Tomorrow, happen what may, we will win!"

"That's right, your excellency! That's the truth, the real truth," said Timokhin. "Who would spare himself now? The soldiers in my battalion—believe me—won't touch their vodka! 'It's not the day for that!' they say."

Everyone fell silent. The officers rose. Prince Andrew went out of the shed with them, giving final orders to the adjutant. After they had gone, Pierre approached Prince Andrew and was about to start talking when they heard the clatter of three horses on the road nearby. Looking in that direction, Prince Andrew recognized Wolzogen and Clausewitz accompanied by a Cossack. They rode close by, still talking, and Prince Andrew involuntarily caught these words:
"The war must be extended across a wide area. I cannot praise that view highly enough," said one of them.
* "The war must be extended widely. I cannot sufficiently commend that view."
"Oh yes," said the other, "the only objective is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot take into account the loss of private individuals."
* "Oh yes, the only aim is to weaken the enemy, so of course one cannot consider the loss of private individuals."
"Oh, no," agreed the other.

"Extend widely!" said Prince Andrew with an angry snort when they had ridden past. "In that 'extend' were my father, son, and sister at Bald Hills. That's all the same to him! That's what I was telling you—those German gentlemen won't win the battle tomorrow, they'll only make as big a mess as they can, because they have nothing in their German heads but theories not worth an empty eggshell, and haven't in their hearts the one thing needed tomorrow—the thing Timokhin has. They've surrendered all of Europe to him, and now they've come to teach us. Fine teachers!" and again his voice went shrill.
"So you think we'll win tomorrow's battle?" asked Pierre.

"Yes, yes," answered Prince Andrew absently. "One thing I would do if I had the power," he began again, "I would not take prisoners. Why take prisoners? It's playing at chivalry! The French have destroyed my home and are on their way to destroy Moscow; they have outraged and continue to outrage me every moment. They are my enemies. In my view they are all criminals. And Timokhin thinks so too, and the whole army. They should be executed! Since they are my enemies, they cannot be my friends, whatever may have been said at Tilsit."
"Yes, yes," muttered Pierre, looking with shining eyes at Prince Andrew. "I completely agree with you!"

The question that had troubled Pierre on the Mozhaysk hill and throughout the day now seemed perfectly clear and fully resolved. He now understood the whole meaning and importance of this war and of the coming battle. Everything he had seen that day, all the significant and serious expressions on the faces he had passed, were illuminated for him by a new light. He understood that latent heat (as they say in physics) of patriotism which was present in all these men he had seen, and this explained why they all prepared for death calmly and almost lightheartedly.

"Not take prisoners," Prince Andrew continued. "That alone would completely change the whole war and make it less cruel. As it is, we've been playing at war—that's what's vile! We play at magnanimity and all that stuff. Such magnanimity and sensitivity are like a lady who faints at the sight of a calf being slaughtered: she is so tenderhearted she can't look at blood, but she enjoys eating the calf served up with sauce. They talk to us about the rules of war, about chivalry, about flags of truce, about mercy to the unfortunate, and so on. It's all rubbish! I saw chivalry and flags of truce in 1805; they deceived us and we deceived them. They plunder other people's homes, circulate counterfeit money, and worst of all they kill my children and my father—and then talk about rules of war and magnanimity to the enemy! Take no prisoners, kill and be killed! Whoever has come to this, as I have, through the same suffering..."

Prince Andrew, who had thought it made no difference to him whether Moscow was taken as Smolensk had been, was suddenly checked by an unexpected cramp in his throat. He paced back and forth a few times in silence, but his eyes glittered feverishly and his lips quivered as he began speaking.

"If there were none of this magnanimity in war, we would go to war only when it was worth going to certain death, as now. Then there would be no war because Paul Ivanovich had offended Michael Ivanovich. And when there was a war like this one, it would be real war! And then the determination of the troops would be completely different. Then all these Westphalians and Hessians whom Napoleon is dragging along would not follow him into Russia, and we would not go fight in Austria and Prussia without knowing why. War is not a polite game but the most horrible thing in life; and we ought to understand that and not play at it. We ought to accept this terrible necessity sternly and seriously. It all comes down to this: get rid of the falsehood and let war be war and not a game. As it is now, war is the favorite pastime of the idle and frivolous. The military profession is the most highly honored."

"But what is war? What is needed for success in warfare? What are the customs of the military? The aim of war is murder; the methods of war are spying, treachery, and their encouragement, the ruin of a country's inhabitants, robbing them or stealing to feed the army, and fraud and falsehood called military strategy. Military life means the absence of freedom—that is, discipline—plus idleness, ignorance, cruelty, debauchery, and drunkenness. And in spite of all this, it is the most esteemed class, respected by everyone. All the kings except the Chinese wear military uniforms, and the man who kills the most people gets the highest rewards."

"They gather, as we shall gather tomorrow, to murder one another; they kill and maim tens of thousands, and then hold thanksgiving services for having killed so many people (they even exaggerate the numbers), and announce a victory, supposing that the more people killed, the greater the achievement. How does God above look down at them and hear them?" exclaimed Prince Andrew in a shrill, piercing voice. "Ah, my friend, it has become hard for me to live of late. I see that I have begun to understand too much. And it isn't good for man to taste of the tree of knowledge of good and evil... Well, it won't be for much longer!" he added.
"However, you're sleepy, and it's time for me to sleep. Go back to Gorki!" said Prince Andrew suddenly.
"Oh no!" Pierre replied, looking at Prince Andrew with frightened, compassionate eyes.
"Go, go! Before a battle one needs a good night's sleep," repeated Prince Andrew.
He came quickly up to Pierre, embraced and kissed him. "Goodbye, be off!" he shouted. "Whether we meet again or not..." and turning away abruptly, he went into the shed.
It was already dark, and Pierre could not tell whether the expression on Prince Andrew's face was angry or tender.

For some time he stood in silence, wondering whether he should follow him or go away. "No, he doesn't want me to!" Pierre decided. "And I know that this is our last meeting!" He sighed deeply and rode back to Gorki.
Re-entering the shed, Prince Andrew lay down on a rug, but he could not sleep.

He closed his eyes. One image succeeded another in his imagination. On one of them he dwelt long and joyfully. He vividly recalled an evening in Petersburg. Natasha, with an animated, excited face, was telling him how she had gone looking for mushrooms the previous summer and had gotten lost in the big forest. She described the depths of the forest, her feelings, and a conversation with a beekeeper she met, incoherently and constantly interrupting her story to say: "No, I can't! I'm not telling it right; no, you don't understand," though he encouraged her by saying that he did understand, and he really had understood all she wanted to say. But Natasha was not satisfied with her own words: she felt they didn't convey the passionately poetic feeling she had experienced that day and wished to share. "He was such a delightful old man, and it was so dark in the forest... and he had such kind... No, I can't describe it," she had said, flushed and excited. Prince Andrew smiled now the same happy smile as he had then when he looked into her eyes. "I understood her," he thought. "I not only understood her, but it was that inner, spiritual force—that sincerity, that openness of soul—that very soul of hers, which seemed bound by her body—it was that soul I loved in her... loved so deeply and happily..." and suddenly he remembered how his love had ended. "He didn't need anything like that. He neither saw nor understood anything of the kind. He only saw in her a pretty, fresh young girl with whom he didn't bother to join his fate. And I?... and he is still alive and happy!"
Prince Andrew jumped up as if someone had burned him, and again began pacing back and forth in front of the shed.

title: Book Eleven (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Helene understood that the question was quite simple from the Church's point of view, and that her spiritual directors were creating difficulties only because they feared how the secular authorities would react.

So she decided to prepare public opinion. She provoked the jealousy of the elderly magnate and told him what she had told the other suitor — that the only way for him to have a claim on her was to marry her. The elderly magnate was at first just as startled by the suggestion of marrying a woman whose husband was still alive as the younger man had been, but Helene's unshakable conviction that it was as simple and natural as marrying a single woman had its effect on him too. Had Helene herself shown the slightest sign of hesitation, shame, or secrecy, her cause would certainly have been lost; but not only did she show no such signs — on the contrary, with good-natured openness she told her close friends (which meant all of Petersburg) that both the prince and the magnate had proposed, and that she loved both and was afraid of hurting either.

A rumor immediately spread through Petersburg — not that Helene wanted to divorce her husband (had such a report spread, many would have opposed so illegal an intention), but simply that the unfortunate and fascinating Helene was torn over which of the two men to marry. The question was no longer whether this was permissible, but only which was the better match and how the court would view it. There were, admittedly, some rigid individuals who could not rise to such heights and who saw the whole scheme as a desecration of the sacrament of marriage, but there weren't many, and they kept quiet. The majority were interested in Helene's good fortune and in the question of which match would be more advantageous. Whether it was right or wrong to remarry while one's husband was living, they did not discuss — that question had obviously been settled by people "wiser than you or me," as they said, and to doubt that decision was to risk exposing one's own stupidity and inability to function in society.

Only Marya Dmitrievna Akhrosimova, who had come to Petersburg that summer to visit one of her sons, allowed herself to express an opinion contrary to the general one. Meeting Helene at a ball, she stopped her in the middle of the room and, amid general silence, said in her gruff voice: "So wives of living men have started marrying again! Maybe you think you've invented something new? You've been beaten to it, my dear! It was thought of long ago. It's done in all the brothels." And with those words, Marya Dmitrievna rolled up her wide sleeves with her usual threatening gesture, glanced sternly around, and marched across the room.

Though people feared Marya Dmitrievna, she was regarded in Petersburg as a buffoon, and of what she'd said they noticed and repeated in whispers only the one crude word she'd used, assuming the entire sting of her remark lay in it.
Prince Vasily, who lately often forgot what he'd said and repeated the same thing a hundred times, remarked to his daughter whenever he happened to see her:

"Helene, I have something to say to you," and he would lead her aside, drawing her hand downward. "I've heard about certain plans concerning... you know. Well, my dear child, you know how your father's heart rejoices to know that you... You have suffered so much. But, my dear child, consult only your own heart. That is all I have to say." And concealing his invariable emotion, he would press his cheek to his daughter's and move away.

Bilibin, who had not lost his reputation as an exceedingly clever man, and who was one of the disinterested male friends that a brilliant woman like Helene always has — friends who can never become lovers — once gave her his view of the matter at a small, private gathering.

"Listen, Bilibin," said Helene (she always called such friends by their last names), touching his coat sleeve with her white, ring-laden fingers. "Tell me, as you would a sister, what I should do. Which of the two?"
Bilibin wrinkled the skin over his eyebrows and thought, smiling.

"You're not catching me off guard, you know," he said. "As a true friend, I've thought and thought about your situation. You see, if you marry the prince" — he meant the younger man, and he crooked one finger — "you lose forever the chance of marrying the other, and you'll displease the court besides. (You know there's some sort of connection.) But if you marry the old count, you'll make his last days happy, and as a widow of the Grand... the prince would no longer be making a poor match by marrying you." And Bilibin smoothed out his forehead.

"That's what a true friend sounds like!" said Helene, beaming, and she touched Bilibin's sleeve again. "But I love them both, you know, and I don't want to hurt either. I would give my life for the happiness of both."
Bilibin shrugged, as if to say that not even he could help with that.
"A masterly woman! That's what's called having it all figured out. She'd like to marry all three at once," he thought.
* A masterly woman.
"But tell me, how will your husband view the matter?" Bilibin asked — his reputation was so well established that he didn't fear asking so blunt a question. "Will he agree?"
"Oh, he loves me so!" said Helene, who for some reason imagined that Pierre too loved her. "He'll do anything for me."
Bilibin pursed his lips in preparation for something witty.
"Even divorce you?" he said.
Helene laughed.

Among those who dared to question the legitimacy of the proposed marriage was Helene's mother, Princess Kuragina. She was constantly tormented by jealousy of her daughter, and now that the jealousy concerned a subject close to her own heart, she couldn't accept the idea. She consulted a Russian priest about the possibility of divorce and remarriage during a husband's lifetime, and the priest told her it was impossible, and to her delight showed her a Gospel passage that (as he saw it) plainly forbids remarriage while the husband lives.
Armed with these arguments, which seemed to her unanswerable, she went to her daughter's early one morning to catch her alone.
Having listened to her mother's objections, Helene smiled blandly and ironically.
"But it says clearly: 'Whosoever shall marry her that is divorced...'" said the old princess.

"Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations," Helene said, switching from Russian — in which she always felt her case didn't sound quite right — to French, which suited it better.
* "Oh, Mama, don't talk nonsense. You don't understand anything. In my position I have obligations."
"But, my dear..."
"Oh, Mama, how can you not understand that the Holy Father, who has the right to grant dispensations..."
Just then the companion who lived with Helene came in to announce that His Highness was in the ballroom and wished to see her.
"No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
* "No, tell him I don't wish to see him. I am furious with him for not keeping his word to me."
"Countess, there is mercy for every sin," said a fair-haired young man with a long face and nose as he entered the room.
* "Countess, there is mercy for every sin."
The old princess rose respectfully and curtsied. The young man who had entered took no notice of her. The princess nodded to her daughter and sidled out of the room.

"Yes, she is right," the old princess thought, all her convictions dissolving at the sight of His Highness. "She is right — but how is it that we, in our irrecoverable youth, didn't know it? Yet it is so simple," she mused as she got into her carriage.

By the beginning of August, Helene's plans were clearly defined, and she wrote a letter to her husband — who, she imagined, loved her very much — informing him of her intention to marry N.N. and of her conversion to the one true faith, and asking him to complete the formalities necessary for a divorce, which would be explained to him by the letter's bearer.
And so I pray God to have you, my friend, in His holy and powerful keeping — Your friend Helene.
This letter was delivered to Pierre's house while he was on the field of Borodino.

title: Book Fifteen (1812 - 13) — Chapter 9
paragraphs: The Fifth Company was camped at the very edge of the forest. A huge campfire blazed brightly in the middle of the snow, lighting up the branches of trees heavy with frost.
Around midnight they heard footsteps in the snow and the cracking of dry branches in the forest.
"A bear, lads," said one of the men.
They all raised their heads to listen, and out of the forest into the bright firelight stepped two strangely dressed human figures clinging to each other.

They were two Frenchmen who had been hiding in the forest. They came up to the fire, hoarsely saying something in a language the Russian soldiers didn't understand. One was taller than the other; he wore an officer's hat and seemed completely exhausted. As he approached the fire and tried to sit down, he fell. The other, a short, sturdy soldier with a shawl tied around his head, was stronger. He lifted his companion and said something, pointing to his mouth. The Russian soldiers gathered around the Frenchmen, spread a greatcoat on the ground for the sick man, and brought buckwheat porridge and vodka for both of them.
The exhausted French officer was Ramballe, and the man with the shawl around his head was Morel, his orderly.

When Morel had drunk some vodka and finished his bowl of porridge, he suddenly became unnaturally cheerful and chattered nonstop to the soldiers, who couldn't understand him. Ramballe refused food and, resting his head on his elbow, lay silent beside the campfire, staring at the Russian soldiers with red, vacant eyes. Occasionally he let out a long groan, then fell silent again. Morel, pointing to his shoulders, tried to convey that Ramballe was an officer and ought to be warmed. A Russian officer who had approached the fire sent to ask his colonel whether he would take a French officer into his hut, and when the messenger returned saying the colonel agreed, Ramballe was told to go. He rose and tried to walk but staggered and would have fallen if a nearby soldier hadn't caught him.
"You won't try that again, eh?" said one of the soldiers, winking and turning mockingly to Ramballe.
"Oh, you fool! Why talk rubbish, you oaf—a real peasant!" came rebukes from every side at the joking soldier.
They surrounded Ramballe, lifted him onto the crossed arms of two soldiers, and carried him to the hut. Ramballe put his arms around their necks as they carried him and began wailing plaintively:
"Oh, you fine fellows, my kind, kind friends! These are real men! Oh, my brave, kind friends!" And he rested his head on one soldier's shoulder like a child.
Meanwhile, Morel was sitting in the best spot by the fire, surrounded by soldiers.

Morel, a short, sturdy Frenchman with inflamed, streaming eyes, wore a woman's cloak and had a shawl tied around his head over his cap, babushka-style. He was clearly tipsy and was singing a French song in a hoarse, broken voice with one arm thrown around the nearest soldier. The soldiers simply held their sides watching him.
"Come on, come on, teach us how it goes! I'll pick it up quick. How does it go?" said a man who was both a singer and a comedian, the one Morel was embracing.
"Long live Henry the Fourth! Long live that brave king!" sang Morel, winking. "That rowdy devil..."
("Long live Henry the Fourth, that valiant king! That rowdy devil.")
"Vivarika! Vif-seruvaru! Sedyablyaka!" the soldier repeated, waving his arm and actually catching the tune.
"Bravo! Ha, ha, ha!" Rough, joyful laughter burst from all sides.
Morel, wrinkling up his face, laughed too.
"Well, go on, go on!"
"Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a charming fellow..."
(Who had a triple talent—for drinking, for fighting, and for being a gallant old boy...)
"Smooth, that is. Come on now, Zaletaev!"
"Ke..." Zaletaev brought out with effort: "ke-e-e-e," he drawled, laboriously pursing his lips, "le-trip-ta-la-de-bu-de-ba, e de-tra-va-ga-la," he sang.
"Fine! Just like the Frenchman! Ho ho ho! Want some more to eat?"
"Give him some porridge—it takes a long time to fill up after you've been starving."

They gave him more porridge and Morel, laughing, set to work on his third bowl. All the young soldiers watched him with beaming smiles. The older men, who considered it beneath their dignity to amuse themselves with such nonsense, continued lying on the other side of the fire, but one would occasionally prop himself up on an elbow and glance at Morel with a smile.
"They're human beings too," said one of them as he wrapped himself in his coat. "Even weeds grow from their own roots."
"Oh Lord, oh Lord! How starry it is! Incredible! That means a hard frost..."

They all fell quiet. The stars, as if knowing that no one was watching them, began to play in the dark sky: now flaring up, now vanishing, now trembling, they whispered among themselves something joyful and mysterious.
